Medicine is somewhat similar: virtually all of the world's pharmaceutical companies are based in the US.

The issue of cost of medical care, aside from the medication aspect that others here have already covered nicely, is also a result of how we handle paying for it. We have institutionalized the middle man, and deliberately created a system in which costs are nebulous and obscured from the consumer - No other industry in the US gets away with this kind of behavior. When you buy a car, there is a sticker price which you can negotiate on. When you shop online, you can compare prices, price match identical services and goods, or get a good idea of value for cost. None of this works in healthcare, and the ACA actually just made things worse.

Real "heathcare" reform (not a "health insurance law") would mandate that care providers make public the actual cost of their services and their objective quality (infection rates, complication rates vs nat. avg) so that when consumers are presented with a price, it has an actual meaning - There is still a role for the insurance industry, but to have an entire healthcare system built upon what is essentially the same premise casino's use to make money is downright absurd.

Also worth noting that the 10 other "developed countries" in the list (based on the 3 examples in the article) are likely on the order of 1/4 the population of the US. It's significantly easier to develop a system in which you don't have to contend with 318 million people spread across a geographic range the size of the US, with substantial rural areas and infrastructure.
